text: Why is the range of a signed byte -128 to +127 rather than -127 to +127?
choices: Because two's complement rounds toward negative infinity, which gains one extra value below zero.
Zero occupies one of the 256 patterns and has only one representation, so the 255 remaining split 128 negative and 127 positive.
Because the sign bit is stored separately, leaving seven bits for magnitude on the positive side only.
Because -128 is a special sentinel value the hardware reserves for overflow detection.
explanation: This is the asymmetry the preface promised a reason for. Sign-magnitude and ones' complement both give two representations of zero — +0 and -0 — which wastes a pattern and forces the adder to handle a special case. Two's complement has exactly one zero, so the leftover pattern goes to the negative side. The asymmetry is the price of a single, uniform zero.
